recent_posts.title: When Planning Should Become A Shared Problem
recent_posts.summary: When leaders request more features than a team can deliver by a deadline, the problem should be treated as shared rather than delegated entirely to the team. Leaders who default to pressure often do so because teams have historically been unreliable, while teams become unreliable partly due to that same pressure — a systemic cycle. Better leaders get curious about what's driving complexity, engage in tradeoff discussions, and help find a 'good-enough' solution such as reducing scope or phasing delivery. Teams, in turn, must build credibility through reliable planning. A real-world example illustrates how a leader simplified a feature by understanding where complexity actually lived, enabling an earlier release. The post also promotes an 'Overcommitment Toolkit for Leaders' with planning worksheets and guides.

recent_posts.title: The Story Critic Skill for Coaching User Stories and Better Refinement
recent_posts.summary: Story Critic is an AI skill for ChatGPT and Claude, developed by Mountain Goat Software, that coaches teams on writing better product backlog items. It evaluates each item on two dimensions: a headline coaching assessment (six levels from 'Not Yet a Story' to 'Ready for Implementation') and backlog placement guidance (whether the detail level is appropriate for near-term or lower-backlog items). The skill focuses on outcome clarity, scope focus, testability, and backlog fit rather than rigid formatting rules. It supports quick critique, full critique, batch review, and rewrite-only output modes. Teams can customize the skill by editing its rubric, adding domain-specific examples, and tuning vocabulary, strictness, and story-splitting preferences. It is available as a downloadable zip for ChatGPT/Claude or through a free Mountain Goat Essentials account.

recent_posts.title: Why teams overcommit and how leaders make it worse
recent_posts.summary: Software teams naturally tend toward optimism in their estimates, which means leadership pressure can push them into dramatic overcommitment. The post distinguishes between forecasts, plans, and commitments — arguing that commitments require margin. It explains how anchoring (framing a desired answer before teams estimate) distorts planning, using a personal story of a product delivery that missed its year-end revenue target by weeks. Leaders are advised to ask open-ended questions like 'When can you do it?' instead of 'Can you do it by X?', to make it psychologically safe to surface risks, and to treat planning as a shared problem rather than delegating it entirely to the team. Repeated overcommitment erodes organizational trust in plans over time.

recent_posts.title: The Cost of Change Curve Is Outdated
recent_posts.summary: Barry Boehm's cost-of-change curve—the idea that late changes in software are exponentially more expensive—was valid in the 1970s-80s but no longer reflects modern reality. Three forces have flattened the curve: modern IDEs and tooling, automated testing and CI, and modular architectures. Agile further reduced costs by shortening feedback cycles, and AI-assisted development is now accelerating that trend again by making code revision dramatically faster. The real bottleneck today is no longer coding effort but feedback delay. The practical implication: teams and managers should stop treating requirements as documents to be perfected upfront, and instead treat them as living artifacts that evolve alongside the product. The biggest risk in modern software development is waiting too long to learn, not changing too late.

recent_posts.title: Estimating and Planning in Agile: Why They Still Matter in 2026
recent_posts.summary: Estimation and planning remain essential in agile development, not for predicting the future but for making informed decisions. Teams that abandon these practices often make implicit estimates anyway, creating hidden assumptions. Effective estimation treats numbers as hypotheses rather than promises, uses ranges instead of single values, and ties every estimate to a specific decision. Flow metrics complement but don't replace estimation, especially for novel work. The key is using estimates to support learning and decision-making rather than as tools for blame or performance evaluation.

recent_posts.title: Why Soft Skills Matter More Than Technical Skills in Agile Teams
recent_posts.summary: Soft skills like collaboration, empathy, and facilitation have lasting value in product development, while technical skills become obsolete every 2-4 years. These interpersonal capabilities reduce risk, improve entire team performance rather than just individuals, and prove most critical under pressure. Roles like Scrum Masters and Product Owners depend heavily on soft skills for facilitation and stakeholder alignment. Organizations should intentionally develop these durable skills through training and coaching, as they compound over time and don't fade when technologies change.

recent_posts.title: How to Use AI for Product Discovery and Writing Better User Stories
recent_posts.summary: AI can accelerate product discovery and backlog refinement by generating personas, conducting mock interviews, creating interview guides for real users, writing user and job stories, adding acceptance criteria, and evaluating story quality against INVEST criteria. The approach uses structured prompts to build detailed personas with hopes, concerns, and decision criteria, then leverages those personas to generate product backlog items and acceptance criteria in both list and Gherkin formats. AI serves as a preparation tool that helps teams arrive better informed for conversations with actual users and stakeholders, not as a replacement for real user research.

recent_posts.title: A checklist to verify if your team is actually doing Scrum
recent_posts.summary: A practical checklist helps teams determine if they're genuinely practicing Scrum or just using the name. The litmus test includes nine must-have basics: sprint length of one month or less, defined Scrum roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers), a sprint goal, daily scrums, usable increments, sprint reviews with stakeholders, sprint retrospectives, and a consistent definition of done. Missing any single element means you're not doing Scrum. The framework also provides deeper validation across nine categories including team structure, product backlog management, sprint cadence, and living the five Scrum values (Focus, Openness, Respect, Commitment, Courage).

recent_posts.title: Why Teams Matter More Than Ever for Innovation
recent_posts.summary: Breakthrough innovation emerges from collaborative teams rather than lone individuals. Research analyzing millions of papers and patents shows team discoveries are six times more likely to be highly referenced. High-performing teams share deep purpose, challenge each other respectfully, create psychological safety, and maintain collective curiosity. Modern product development requires cross-functional teams that think together, debate assumptions, and build on diverse perspectives. Leaders should invest in stable teams, psychological safety, discovery time, and purpose-driven work to unlock creative potential.
